# Information, precision and reliability {#information}

<div class="goals">
**Learning goals.** After this chapter you can

* read item and test information curves;
* convert information into a conditional standard error of measurement;
* compute marginal and empirical reliability, and explain why a single
  reliability coefficient hides how precision changes along the scale;
* use information to judge whether a test is well targeted for a decision.
</div>

**Key terms:**
[item information](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#item-information),
[test information](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#test-information),
[standard error of measurement](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#standard-error-of-measurement),
[marginal reliability](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#marginal-reliability),
[targeting](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#targeting),
[precision](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#precision).

## The ideas

In classical test theory a test has one standard error of measurement for
everyone. In IRT, precision depends on where you are on the scale. An item
tells us most about people whose ability is close to its difficulty: for
them the outcome is most uncertain, so observing it is most informative. The
**item information function** of a 2PL item is

$$I_j(\theta) = a_j^2 \, P_j(\theta)\,[1 - P_j(\theta)],$$

which peaks at $\theta = b_j$, where $P_j = 0.5$, with height $a_j^2/4$. A
steep item gives a lot of information in a narrow range; a flat item a
little information over a wide range. For the 3PL the peak is lower and a
little above $b_j$, because guessing makes correct answers less informative.

Information adds up over items. The **test information function** is the sum
of the item information functions, and the **conditional standard error** of
a $\theta$ estimate is approximately

$$SE(\theta) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{I(\theta)}}.$$

So doubling the information shrinks the standard error by a factor of
$\sqrt{2}$, not 2. A test information of 10 gives $SE \approx 0.32$, and on a
scale with standard deviation 1 that corresponds to a reliability of about
$1 - 0.32^2 = 0.90$ for people at that point.

Two summary reliability coefficients are common:

* **Marginal reliability** averages the error variance over the assumed
  population distribution of $\theta$: $\rho = 1 - \overline{SE^2}/\sigma^2_\theta$.
* **Empirical reliability** does the same with the estimated scores and
  their standard errors in the sample.

Both are useful single numbers, but a test can have a respectable overall
reliability and still be imprecise exactly where an important decision is
made. That is why we look at the curves.

## Example 1: where does the science test measure well?

```{r data-information-1}
# SAT12 science items, scored with the corrected key (item 32 keyed 3).
key <- c(1,4,5,2,3,1,2,1,3,1,2,4,2,1,5,3,4,4,1,4,3,3,4,1,3,5,1,3,1,5,4,3)
resp <- key2binary(SAT12, key)
```

```{r}
mod <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE)
gg_info(mod) + gg_info(mod, type = "se")
```

The test is most informative a little below average ability and loses
precision quickly above $\theta = 1$. The values behind the curves:

```{r}
theta <- matrix(-3:3)
data.frame(theta = theta[, 1],
           information = testinfo(mod, theta),
           se = 1 / sqrt(testinfo(mod, theta)))
```

Each item's contribution:

```{r, fig.height = 4.6}
gg_info(mod, type = "items", which.items = c(1, 6, 9, 12, 19, 28))
```

Items differ a lot. Steep items in the middle of the scale do most of the
work; very easy items (such as Item.9) add information only far below
average, and flat items (such as Item.12) add almost nothing anywhere.

Reliability:

```{r}
marginal_rxx(mod)
empirical_rxx(fscores(mod, full.scores.SE = TRUE))
```

`areainfo()` tells us how much of the test's total information lies in a
range of the scale, here between $\theta = -1$ and $\theta = 1$:

```{r}
areainfo(mod, c(-1, 1))
```

Suppose the school awards a science prize to students above $\theta = 1.5$.
At that point the standard error is

```{r}
1 / sqrt(testinfo(mod, matrix(1.5)))
```

about half a standard deviation. A student estimated at 1.5 could easily
have a true ability of 1.0 or 2.0. The overall reliability of about 0.84
gives a much rosier picture than the precision at the decision point.

## Example 2: designing a test for a decision

Information curves are also a design tool. Imagine a calibrated pool of 90
2PL items for a nursing entrance test, with a pass mark at $\theta = 0.5$.
We compare three 20-item forms built from the pool, without collecting any
new data: the information function only needs the item parameters.

```{r data-information-2}
# A pool of 90 calibrated 2PL items (a, b), as stored in an item bank.
# No responses are needed: this example works from item parameters only.
set.seed(606)
pool <- data.frame(item = sprintf("N%02d", 1:90),
                   a = rlnorm(90, 0.15, 0.3),
                   b = rnorm(90, -0.3, 1.1))
```

A small function computes 2PL information from the formula above:

```{r}
info_2pl <- function(items, theta) {
  sapply(theta, function(t) {
    p <- plogis(items$a * (t - items$b))
    sum(items$a^2 * p * (1 - p))
  })
}
```

Three ways to choose 20 items:

```{r}
forms <- list(
  random   = pool[sample(nrow(pool), 20), ],
  spread   = pool[order(pool$b)[round(seq(1, 90, length.out = 20))], ],
  targeted = pool[order(abs(pool$b - 0.5) / pool$a)[1:20], ]
)
grid <- seq(-3, 3, by = 0.05)
curves <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(forms), function(f)
  data.frame(form = f, theta = grid, info = info_2pl(forms[[f]], grid))))
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(curves, aes(theta, info, colour = form)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = 2) +
  labs(x = expression(theta), y = "Test information", colour = "Form") +
  theme_mirtverse()
```

The *targeted* form picks items whose difficulty is close to the pass mark,
favouring steep ones (dividing by $a$ ranks steep items first). The *spread*
form covers the whole range evenly, and the *random* form is what we get by
chance. At the pass mark:

```{r}
sapply(forms, function(f) c(info = info_2pl(f, 0.5), se = 1 / sqrt(info_2pl(f, 0.5))))
```

The targeted form has more than twice as much information at the pass mark as the
random one, with the same number of items. The price is precision far from
the cut: the spread form is better for reporting scores across the whole
range. Which is better depends on what the scores are for. A licensing test
cares about the pass mark; a progress test cares about everyone. Chapter
\@ref(banks-cat) builds on this idea with automated test assembly and
adaptive testing.

## Your turn

<div class="yourturn">
1. Show, using `info_2pl()` and a single item with $a = 2$, $b = 0$, that the
   information peaks at $\theta = 0$ with height $a^2/4 = 1$.
2. In Example 1, how many items like the average SAT12 item would you need
   to add to bring the standard error at $\theta = 1.5$ down to 0.35?
3. In Example 2, build a 30-item targeted form. How much does the standard
   error at the pass mark improve over the 20-item targeted form?
4. Explain to a colleague why "the test has a reliability of 0.84" is not
   enough to decide whether it can be used to award the prize.
</div>

<details><summary>Solutions</summary>

```{r}
one <- data.frame(a = 2, b = 0)
grid[which.max(info_2pl(one, grid))]; max(info_2pl(one, grid))

# 2. information needed for SE = 0.35, and the average item information at 1.5
need <- 1 / 0.35^2
have <- testinfo(mod, matrix(1.5))
per_item <- have / 32
ceiling((need - have) / per_item)

t30 <- pool[order(abs(pool$b - 0.5) / pool$a)[1:30], ]
1 / sqrt(c(twenty = info_2pl(forms$targeted, 0.5), thirty = info_2pl(t30, 0.5)))
```

2. Many more items, because the average item adds little information at
   1.5. Adding a few *hard, discriminating* items would be far more
   efficient than adding average ones.
4. Reliability is an average over everybody. The prize decision happens at
   $\theta = 1.5$, where the test has much less information than in the
   middle; what matters is the standard error there.

</details>

## Further reading {-}

Lord [-@lord1980] introduced information functions as a tool for test
construction; Hambleton, Swaminathan and Rogers [-@hambleton1991] give an
accessible account. van der Linden [-@vanderlinden2005] shows how to build
tests to target information curves.
